days.brief: Starting point for the whole path. Read it as a catalogue: skim the mechanisms (domain changes, localisation signals, NMD, UTR effects) and note two or three examples you'd want to look for in your own isoform data. Tomorrow's papers on proteome expansion and the Tress/Blencowe debate lean on this vocabulary.
days.summary: A long review that catalogues what alternative splicing does to the proteins it produces. It goes mechanism by mechanism: changes to binding domains and interaction partners, enzymatic activity, subcellular localisation, stability and post-translational modification. It also covers isoforms that are never translated because a premature stop codon sends them to nonsense-mediated decay.
takeaways: Splicing rarely switches a protein fully on or off. More often it adds or removes a short module (a binding motif, a localisation signal, a modification site) that changes how the protein is regulated.
Many alternative exons are short and encode disordered regions, so their effect is easy to miss if you only look at folded domains.
A large share of isoform changes act on the RNA rather than the protein, through decay or changed untranslated regions, so a shift in isoform proportions does not always mean a new protein.
days.relevance: This is the biological reason to model isoform proportions within a gene separately from gene totals, as your NB + multinomial factorisation does. The mechanisms it lists are roughly the consequences IsoformSwitchAnalyzeR annotates (domain loss, signal peptides, disordered regions, NMD sensitivity), so they are the natural way to interpret any isoform shift your generative model or scIso predicts.

discover.title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction (SynGeneFlow)
discover.summary: For combinatorial perturbations, most of the response is the sum of single-perturbation effects. SynGeneFlow anchors the flow's source distribution at that additive prior and learns only the residual flow to the true perturbed state.
takeaways: Choosing an informative source distribution focuses model capacity on the hard, non-additive part of the signal.
Gene-gene interactions enter as a static mask plus a perturbation-dependent bias in the network.
MMD regularisation on both the endpoint and the residual distributions keeps population-level structure.
discover.relevance: Same design question as your source-conditioned models: what to put at t = 0. A gene-level prediction (as in scIso) could serve as the source, with the flow learning only the isoform-level residual.

discover.title: Large Flow Language Models (Lafa)
discover.summary: A continuous flow language model scaled to 8B parameters by adapting a pretrained autoregressive model: causal attention over the prefix and bidirectional, asynchronous flow within each block. Trained on fewer than 30B tokens.
takeaways: Matches or beats the autoregressive base on instruction following, reasoning and coding, and can be distilled into flow maps for one- or few-step generation.
Flow training acts like multi-token prediction and can even improve the AR capabilities it starts from.
A self-speculative decoding scheme (flow drafts, AR verification in one model) gives about 2.5x AR throughput and beats discrete diffusion at comparable quality.
discover.relevance: The current argument for continuous flows over discrete diffusion on discrete data. Useful context for your choice between a CTMC on the lattice simplex and continuous simplex flows, and it connects to the flow-map papers already on your path.

discover.title: VampPrior Unleashed
discover.summary: Revisits the VampPrior, which approximates the optimal VAE prior (the aggregate posterior) with a mixture of encoder outputs at learned pseudo-inputs. It fixes two weaknesses: prior and posterior share one amortised covariance, and the mixture weights are fixed and uniform.
takeaways: Decoupling the prior and posterior covariances removes a conflict between wanting high-entropy priors and low-entropy posteriors, and raises model evidence.
Replacing the uniform mixture with a Dirichlet process gives non-parametric clustering in latent space.
Dropping the new prior into scVI improves integration and clustering across six single-cell atlases. Only the prior changes, so it works with any continuous-latent DLVM.
discover.relevance: A cheap upgrade to try in your hierarchical NB + multinomial VAE baseline: swap the standard normal prior for this one and compare ELBOs and cell-type clustering. David Knowles also works on splicing (LeafCutter), so his group may follow up on isoform-level models.
